scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance emerged around 1910 in the United States, with many sources pointing to the San Francisco underworld and African American communities as its source.
It was part of a broader 'animal dance' trend that included the Turkey Trot and Bunny Hug.
Its popularity was cemented by Irving Berlin's 1910 song 'The Dance of the Grizzly Bear.'
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance served as a playful break from social conventions, offering 'immediate physical pleasure' through movement.
For young immigrants, it was a way to assert American identity, while for critics, it symbolized moral regression and 'sexual excitement.'
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers perform a swaying gait with feet turned outward, mimicking a bear.
The posture involves a close, chest-to-chest embrace with arms resting on the partner's shoulders and fingers curled like claws.
It features lateral hip oscillations, forward rocking of the torso, and syncopated walking steps that allow for improvisation.
Watch for Bear-like embrace, Swaying gait, The Spiel.

Formation: Closed couple; moving in small circles (pivoting) or progressing along the floor.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to ragtime music, characterized by syncopation and displaced accents over a steady bass pattern.
Key instruments include the piano, often played in a style where the right hand syncopates while the left maintains a regular beat.
Listen for the Piano, Voice.
The pulse is 2/4 or 4/4 (Ragtime).

Ragtime music characterized by 'ragged time' where the melody is heavily syncopated and accents are displaced. The sound is driven by a steady, marching bass pattern on the piano, while the vocal versions feature humorous, fast-paced lyrics often delivered in a vaudevillian style.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Originally practiced in urban dance halls and 'rackets' associated with nightlife and popular entertainment.
In high society settings, it was performed in formal attire but with a parodic, 'loufoque' tone.
In France, it was featured in music halls and films.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Irving Berlin composed the most famous songs for the dance.
Performers like Sophie Tucker, Fanny Brice, and Stella Mayhew featured it in vaudeville.
In San Francisco, it was linked to the 'tough' underworld.
It belongs to the 'animal dance' family of the early 20th century.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Grizzly Bear is sibling of Turkey Trot: Often used interchangeably with the Grizzly Bear as part of the animal dance craze.
Grizzly Bear is child of Foxtrot: The Grizzly Bear's walking variations anticipated the development of the foxtrot.
Grizzly Bear is influence of Waltz: The Grizzly Bear emerged as a parodic rupture from the formal conventions of the waltz.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Close embrace, chest-to-chest; torso and abdomen thrust forward beyond normal posture; knees slightly bent.
Arms resting loosely on partner's shoulders; fingers curled to suggest animal paws or claws; leading arm sometimes held rigid and thrust forward.
Pronounced lateral hip oscillations; forward rocking of the torso; wriggling of the trunk.
